questions.title: Does Minnesota Statute § 181.101(a) expressly authorize private employees to recover statutory penalties for wage violations?
questions.question_body: In *Cohen v. Consilio*, the Eighth Circuit affirmed summary judgment on the MPWA claim because the employee cannot seek 'average daily wage penalties.' The opinion relies heavily on the plain language of § 181.101(a) referencing 'the Commissioner.' However, I'm confused about the methodology here. If the statute says 'the Commissioner may charge and collect... any money collected... shall be paid to the employee,' does that imply the employee's right to suing is irrelevant to the penalty itself? Is this a 'jurisdictional' bar or a substantive one that precludes the employee from ever bringing this specific claim to federal court?

questions.title: Can a plaintiff maintain standing to seek statutory penalties under the MFLSA after stipulating to the payment of all wages and liquidated damages?
questions.question_body: The opinion vacates the district court's judgment on the MFLSA claim due to mootness concerns. Cohen stipulated he was paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages, yet the court found a serious concern regarding jurisdiction to decide statutory penalties. But how does the stipulation affect *standing*? If the violation (underpayment) was 'cured' by payment, why does the court insist on the 'claim for civil penalties'? Is it because penalties are punitive/continuing rather than compensatory? I'm struggling to reconcile how payment of back wages leaves the threshold standing issue unresolved when the injury (unpaid wages) is seemingly mitigated.

questions.title: Why is a lack of legal authority or argument in the briefing grounds for waiver in a summary judgment appeal?
questions.question_body: I find the court's treatment of the MWTA claim puzzling. The opinion states, 'Cohen does not dispute that... he is entitled to penalties' but has 'no statutory authority' or 'meaningful argument' in support of reversal. The court then cited *Milligan* stating, 'he has waived the issue.' Does this mean that if a state-law statute was implicit, the federal court can still guess it regardless of the lack of briefing? Or is this an application of the rule that appellate courts are generally not 'correcting errors' if the appellant fails to marshal the necessary legal theory in the brief as per *Fed. R. App. P. 28*?

questions.title: Under what circumstances does a change in requests for injunctive relief during briefing constitute an impermissible 'new claim'?
questions.question_body: The Eighth Circuit vacated the appeal without addressing Cohen's request for injunctive relief that Consilio rescind its policy. Cohen allegedly 'changed course' in his summary judgment briefing compared to the original complaint. The court applied the *InfoDeli* rule that 'new claims are properly raised through amended complaints, not opposition briefs.' But isn't injunctive relief involving the same cause of action? Why does the fact that it is an affirmative equitable remedy change it categorically compared to a legal claim for damages?

questions.title: What is the specific 'voluntary cessation' standard an employer must meet to moot a claim under *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw*?
questions.question_body: The district court remanded for jurisdictional determination on the MFLSA claim because of the *Laidlaw* mootness concern. The opinion notes that while voluntary cessation does not always deprivewith jurisdiction, the employer must show 'it is absolutely clear that its wrongful conduct will not recur.' I need clarification: must the employer prove the policy is dead, or just that the practice is ended? Given Consilio paid Cohen all wages he alleged were owed, is the employer's 'cessation of a challenged practice' a sufficient affirmative defense to establish standing for the penalties if the policy remains official?

questions.title: Why did the 8th Circuit remand specifically for a 'continuing interest' determination rather than simply ruling on the merits of the MFLSA penalties?
questions.question_body: The Eighth Circuit held that the requisite personal interest must continue and vacated the grant of summary judgment regarding the MFLSA penalties, remanding for the district court to determine 'jurisdiction.' Why not resolve whether the case is moot de novo? If the employer stipulated to paying wages, shouldn't the continuing obligation to pay penalties be a question for the judge to decide rather than an appellate court to remand? In *Laidlaw*, the Supreme Court allowed officials to prove cessation, so why does this Eighth Circuit opinion require a jurisdictional 'light most favorable' review on remand rather than an appellate ruling?

questions.title: Does the concurrence's disagreement with the majority regarding attorney's fees suggest a conflict in the 'Article III' standing requirement?
questions.question_body: The concurring opinion by Judge Kobes is clear that he would vacate the judgment and remand for mootness but specifically 'disagrees' regarding attorney's fees, stating 'Neither party briefed the issue.' I am trying to understand if this implies that while the main holding focuses on mootness, the remedies are procedural rather than substantive. If Cohen had already stipulated to receiving all liquidated damages and wages under the stipulation, is the distinction between those and attorney's fees typically considered separately in class-action contexts? Does the concurrence suggest that standing is an independent bar to fees even if standing exists for the penalty claim?
